newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul pledges drastic steps to combat economic ills.
newsitem.headline: Seoul pledges drastic steps to combat economic ills.

text.p: South Korea's new finance minister acknowledged on Thursday the economy was in serious trouble, battered by a trade deficit, labour unrest, bankruptcies and a political crisis.
In a blunt assessment of the economic outlook, Kang Kyong-shik said drastic measures were needed to solve deep-rooted problems.
"There is no doubt the Korean economy is currently in serious trouble," Kang told a news conference.

He said labour strikes over a controversial labour bill rammed through parliament last December, the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co in January and a subsequent political crisis had "all added more uncertainties and instabilities into the economy".
Kang was drafted in to the cabinet last month to clear up the mess and to steady financial markets rocked by South Korea's biggest corporate failure.
The collapse of Hanbo under $5.8 billion in debt uncovered a bribery scandal that has dragged in several of President Kim Young-sam's closest aides and his son.
A key provision of the labour bill making worker layoffs easier has since been watered down.
Since taking office, Kang has stressed fiscal belt-tightening to curb demand and bring down a ballooning current account deficit.

This week, his ministry announced plans to expand foreign investment in the bond and stock markets and a policy to boost overseas borrowing to attract foreign capital and shore up the local currency, the won.
"The Korean government will take all necessary steps to ensure stability in the domestic financial market, and further to ensure Korea's credibility in the international financial market," Kang said.
Kang said danger signals began flashing last year when the current account deficit jumped and slowing economic growth led to a financial crunch and bankruptcies.

He noted that much of the deficit was due to a sharp downturn in the terms of trade, fuelled by plunging prices of exports, including semiconductors. The deficit hit an all-time high of $23.72 billion last year.
"The fear is that there may be a further decline in the balance of payments as the economy's structural problems take a toll on the country's international competitiveness," he said.
To overcome the problems it was crucial to refrain from trying to stimulate the economy soon," he added.
A "high-cost and low-efficiency" structure had been nurtured by heavy-handed government regulation. "We need drastic measures to solve that problem," he said.
"What is called for is deregulation and promotion of competition."
Kang noted the government planned to slash two trillion won ($2.2 billion) from this year's budget and lower tax revenue by an equal amount to help reduce demand.
Energy prices would remain high to encourage conservation and reduce imports. Energy imports have been a major factor behind the soaring trade deficit.
Kang rejected U.S. criticisms that a "frugality" campaign led by civic groups against consumption of foreign luxury goods was in fact an anti-import drive sponsored by the government.

"The campaign is not something led by the government," he said. Kang also rejected U.S. assertions that South Korea has unfairly stepped in with subsidies to Hanbo Steel, the nation's second largest steelmaker.
